passage:
"Papa! Papa!" Usha's whisper cracked in the dark.
Imran came in, rubbing his eyes. "What is it?"
"There is a monster on the wall. It has big ears."
He did not laugh. "That looks scary from where you are lying. My heart would beat fast too."
"Is it really there?"
"I am going to sit with you." He plugged in the little star light and lowered himself onto the edge of her bed. "Want a hug?"
She nodded into his shoulder. "Are you staying?"
"Until your eyes are heavy."
Her fingers slowly let go of his sleeve.

qa.q: What did Usha say was on the wall?
qa.a: She said there was a monster on the wall with big ears.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she called for Papa?
qa.a: She was frightened, because the monster felt real to her, and her whisper cracked as she called.

qa.q: What did Imran do that helped more than telling her there was nothing?
qa.a: He did not laugh, named how scary it looked, put on a night light, hugged her and stayed until she was sleepy.

qa.q: How might Imran see Usha's fear?
qa.a: He takes it seriously as real to her, since he says his own heart would beat fast too.

grounding: A child sees monsters in the shadows at night, and the parent does not laugh but uses a night light, a hug and calm words and stays.

passage:
Thunder cracked over the fields and the tin roof rattled. Gautam dropped his toy bullock cart, ran across the mud floor and jumped into Nikita's lap.
"I am here," she said, wrapping both arms around him.
She rocked slowly while the rain drummed. His breath, fast at first, began to slow.
When the next rumble came he only gripped the end of her sari and said, "Loud."
"Very loud," Nikita agreed.
After a while he slid down, picked up his cart and pushed it along the floor beside her.

qa.q: What did Gautam drop when the thunder cracked?
qa.a: He dropped his toy bullock cart.

qa.q: How does Gautam feel after Nikita holds him?
qa.a: He feels calm and trusting: his breathing slows and he goes back to playing beside her. 🙂

qa.q: What would you say to someone who thinks holding a scared child makes him weak?
qa.a: Gautam's calm shows that comfort helps: he grips her sari and says it is loud without panicking the second time, so he is learning to settle himself.

qa.q: What might it be like for Nikita when Gautam runs to her?
qa.a: She probably feels needed and wants to reassure him, since she wraps both arms around him at once and stays.

grounding: A child runs to the parent after thunder, is held and told 'I am here', and feels calm.

passage:
Samir clung to his mother's leg at the gate of the new school, his tummy aching. The corridor smelled of paint and the classroom door looked very big.
"I don't want to go in."
Francis, the class teacher, crouched to his level. "It is okay to be scared. We will go slowly. Do you want to just look at the fish tank by the door?"
Samir edged forward one step and peeked. Three orange fish drifted past.
"Can I say hello to them?"
"Yes." Francis waited while Samir let go of his mother's leg and, holding the tank's edge, whispered hello.

qa.q: What did Francis suggest looking at first?
qa.a: Francis suggested looking at the fish tank by the door.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling at the school gate?
qa.a: He was scared: his tummy ached and he clung to his mother's leg, saying he did not want to go in.

qa.q: What small step helped Samir go forward?
qa.a: Francis accepted the fear, promised to go slowly, and offered one small brave step, looking at the fish, which led to saying hello to them. 🙂

qa.q: What might it be like for Samir's mother in that moment?
qa.a: She may feel worried for him but relieved that Francis is patient, since Samir lets go of her leg without being pushed.

grounding: A child is scared of the first day in a new class, his tummy hurts and he clings; the adult says it is okay to be scared and offers a small brave step.

passage:
On the village school ground, a white sheet hung between two poles for the open-air film. When the dark forest music began, Reena pulled her dupatta over her eyes.
A hand found hers. It was Yusuf's, sticky from peanuts. He said nothing, only squeezed.
Her breath came easier and she peeked through her fingers. "It's only a film," he whispered, not letting go.
Later, when a loud clap of thunder sounded in the story, Yusuf flinched. This time Reena held his hand tight.

qa.q: What did Yusuf's hand feel like?
qa.a: It was sticky from peanuts.

qa.q: How did Reena feel when Yusuf held her hand?
qa.a: She felt less alone and calmer: her breathing eased and she dared to peek through her fingers. 🙂

qa.q: What might Reena take from this moment?
qa.a: She may learn that a quiet hand can comfort a scared friend, which she then does for Yusuf at the thunder scene.

qa.q: Why might Yusuf have taken Reena's hand without speaking?
qa.a: He may have noticed she was scared and wanted her to feel supported, and his own flinch later suggests he knows how scary it can be.

grounding: A friend holds the child's hand during the scary part of the film, and she feels less alone and later does the same.

passage:
"Papa, there is something under the bed."
"Under the bed? Ha! Don't be a baby, Sonali. There is nothing there."
"But I heard it."
"Go to sleep." Saurabh chuckled and switched off the light.
Sonali pulled the blanket over her head and held her breath.
The next night he called from the door, "All okay, Sonali?"
"Yes," she said in a small voice, though her heart was thumping.

qa.q: Where did Sonali say the something was?
qa.a: She said it was under the bed.

qa.q: Why did Sonali say yes when Saurabh asked if all was okay?
qa.a: She felt ashamed after being called a baby, so she hid her fear and stayed quiet even though her heart was thumping.

qa.q: What could Saurabh try instead?
qa.a: He could believe her, sit with her, and look under the bed together calmly so she feels heard and the fear gets smaller.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see the moment?
qa.a: He probably thinks it is harmless teasing and does not realise it made her stop telling him.

grounding: A parent laughs at a child's fear and says there is nothing there; she feels ashamed and hides her fear.

passage:
In the block corner of the nursery, Suraj set the last block on top and his tower wobbled, then stood.
"Look at me! I did it all by myself!"
Wasim, the teacher, came over and crouched down. "I see. You put the big blocks at the bottom and the small ones on top. You worked hard on it."
Suraj rose on tiptoe, chest out, and beamed. Then he grabbed a handful of blocks from the box.
"Now I make it taller!"

qa.q: Which blocks did Suraj put at the bottom of the tower?
qa.a: He put the big blocks at the bottom.

qa.q: What is Suraj feeling when he shouts "look at me"?
qa.a: He feels tall, happy and proud, which shows in his tiptoes, out-pushed chest and beam. 🙂

qa.q: Why was Wasim's reply useful for Suraj?
qa.a: Wasim described what was there and named the hard work, so the pride felt real and Suraj wanted to try something bigger.

qa.q: How might Wasim see Suraj's tower?
qa.a: Wasim seems to see real effort and thinking in it, pointing out the big blocks below and small ones above.

grounding: A child builds a tower alone and shouts 'look at me', and the teacher describes what is there and names the hard work.

passage:
"Mummy, look!" Ritu held up her paper. "A bus!"
"Oh, I love it," said Mummy. "And look at all these windows. You gave every person a different hat."
"That is the driver. He has a stripey one."
"How did you get the wheels so round?"
"I traced the bowl."
Zubin, her little brother, hopped up. "Me too?"
"You can draw yours next," said Mummy.
Ritu grinned, glowing. "I will stick it on the fridge myself."

qa.q: How did Ritu make the wheels so round?
qa.a: She traced the bowl.

qa.q: How does Ritu feel when Mummy looks at the drawing?
qa.a: She feels a warm glow of pride, and it grows as Mummy notices details, so she wants to display it herself. 🙂

qa.q: What did Mummy do that a wise parent would do?
qa.a: She noticed specific details like the windows and hats and asked a question about the wheels, rather than only saying good.

qa.q: What might Zubin be feeling as he hops up?
qa.a: He seems keen to join in and share the attention, and Mummy's reply shows his turn is coming.

grounding: A parent looks at the child's drawing and shows love for it by noticing details, and the child feels a warm glow.

passage:
In the school hall after assembly, Ayesha held up her shiny helper-of-the-week badge. "Look, Rehan!"
Rehan's smile faded and he looked at the floor. The badge felt heavier in her hand. She did not know why he was sad.
Keerthana, the teacher, watched from the doorway and said nothing.
Ayesha thought for a moment. "You can get one too. What are you making today?"
"A clay elephant," Rehan mumbled.
"Can I see it?"
He brightened a little and led her to the shelf.

qa.q: What did Ayesha hold up in the hall?
qa.a: She held up her shiny helper-of-the-week badge.

qa.q: How does Ayesha feel when Rehan looks at the floor?
qa.a: She feels confused: she does not know why he is sad, and the badge suddenly feels heavier.

qa.q: What did Ayesha do that kept the friendship warm?
qa.a: She told him he could get one too and asked about his own clay elephant, so the moment was about him as well.

qa.q: How might Rehan see Ayesha's badge at first?
qa.a: He seems sad and perhaps envious, since his smile fades and he looks away from it.

grounding: A child shows her badge and her friend looks away sadly; she is confused, then says he can get one too and asks about his work.

passage:
Valentina held up her painting of a blue cat. "Look!"
Her sister Mei glanced over. "Mine is better," she said, waving her purple house.
Valentina's arm sank and she pressed the paper against her chest.
Dad came in from the hallway and looked at both. "Valentina, that cat has such a big smile, and you mixed a blue I have not seen before. Mei, your house has tiny windows with curtains. That took you a long time. I like both."
"But which is better?" Mei asked.
"I am not choosing. They are different, and each shows your own effort."
Slowly, Valentina lifted her cat again.

qa.q: What did Valentina paint?
qa.a: She painted a blue cat.

qa.q: How does Valentina feel after Mei says hers is better?
qa.a: She feels smaller and hurt: her arm sinks and she hugs the paper to her chest.

qa.q: What did Dad do to keep pride from becoming a contest?
qa.a: He praised each girl for her own effort and details, and refused to rank the paintings.

qa.q: Why might Mei want to know which is better?
qa.a: She may be eager for approval and want to be first, since she asks Dad to pick even after he praises hers.

grounding: A child shows her work and her sister says 'mine is better'; the parent praises each child's own effort.

passage:
I'm Amandeep, the assistant in the nursery class. During story time I noticed Chandrika go very still, then a dark patch spread on her skirt. Her face crumpled and tears ran down. A couple of children turned round.
The teacher moved close without a word, rested a hand on her shoulder and murmured that accidents happen to many children. They walked her out with a shawl round her waist. I read on louder so the class kept looking at the book.
When Chandrika came back in dry clothes, she sat at the back, red-eyed. I can't say what she felt, but she held the picture book I gave her very tightly.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do while the teacher took Chandrika out?
qa.a: Amandeep read on louder so the class kept looking at the book.

qa.q: What was Chandrika probably feeling when the dark patch spread on her skirt?
qa.a: She was probably deeply embarrassed and wanted to vanish, since her face crumpled and she cried, although Amandeep cannot be sure.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped?
qa.a: They helped quietly, wrapped a shawl round her, got her dry clothes and said accidents happen to many children, without drawing attention.

qa.q: How might the teacher have wanted Chandrika to feel when murmuring that accidents happen?
qa.a: The teacher probably wanted Chandrika to feel less ashamed and not singled out, which is why the teacher moved close without a word and said accidents happen to many children.

grounding: A child has an accident in class and feels ashamed; the teacher helps quietly with a change of clothes and no fuss.
